title: Twenty-Four Copies: the Milanese Engraver, Ediciones Urania, and Fifty Years of Buenos Aires Paper
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Milan, and the Crossing That Left No Record

stops.name: Milan, born on the eighth of August
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Library of Congress Name Authority File no2023125659 carries mads:birthDate 1913-08-08 and mads:birthPlace Milan (Italy), sourced to an Argentine art reference consulted 13 November 2023.
stops.campa: In Milan, on the eighth of August, a son is born to a family the reachable record does not name. One line of catalogue data will eventually hold the whole span: Veroni, Raúl, 1913-1992, with the occupations artist and lithographer and the demographic term Argentines. Three of those four facts are earned on another continent. Milan gives him the birth date and the word Italian, which is the word Buenos Aires will still be using for him thirty years later, when he founds a press and prints the first book under his own imprint.
stops.quote: Veroni, Raúl; born in Milan, Italy August 8, 1913; died Buenos Aires, 1992
stops.quote_source: Arte de Argentina, cited as the source note in Library of Congress Name Authority File record no2023125659
suggested_refs: LoC Name Authority File record no2023125659, the single document holding both ends of his life
sources: Library of Congress Name Authority File, no2023125659

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the crossing that left no record
stops.date_confidence: gap. No arrival date, vessel, port, or reason is attested in anything reachable. 1939 is a bracket set by the 1940 commission below, not a record, and the stop is placed on the far shore because that is the only shore the evidence touches.
stops.campa: Between the Milan birth record and the first Buenos Aires book there is nothing: no ship, no port, no year of arrival, no reason. He is Italian in 1913 and he is working in Buenos Aires by 1940, and the passage between the two is documented nowhere reachable. Argentina in these years takes in Italians by the hundred thousand, and the Library of Congress will one day file him under the descriptor Argentines without recording the day he became one. The crossing is marked on the far shore, where the evidence lands, and the gap stands as a gap.
suggested_refs: Argentine immigration registers of the 1930s, unsearched for this journey
sources: Library of Congress Name Authority File, no2023125659

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first traceable commission
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by a bookseller's listing only; no copy has been examined for this journey.
stops.campa: His first traceable Buenos Aires work is an illustration job for an antiquarian's book: La Virgen de la Asunción y su Oratorio, by R. de Lafuente Machain, printed in the city. He is twenty-six or twenty-seven. The commission tells almost nothing about him except the one thing that will hold for the next four decades: somebody in Buenos Aires already knows that if a book needs a plate cut, this Italian can cut it. No copy of the edition has been examined here; the record is a dealer's catalogue line and nothing more.
suggested_refs: R. de Lafuente Machain, La Virgen de la Asunción y su Oratorio, Buenos Aires 1940

stops.name: Buenos Aires, an Italian engraver of thirty
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the house's own history gives the age and the trade but no month.
stops.campa: The house he is about to found describes him in its own history in eight words: Italian, engraver, thirty years old. No training is named, no master, no academy, no Milanese workshop. The phrase artista grabador is a trade description rather than a title; it means a man who works the plate himself and does not merely draw for another to cut. Thirty is the age at which he stops being the hand a publisher hires and becomes the publisher who hires the hands.
stops.quote: Raoul Veroni, italiano, artista grabador, de treinta años de edad
suggested_refs: The Ediciones Urania blog, the only surviving narrative account of the house

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Ediciones Urania founded on Alberti
stops.date_confidence: year attested by the house history; the month is not recorded anywhere and June is placement only.
stops.campa: He founds Ediciones Urania and finances its first book himself: Rafael Alberti's Tres Recuerdos del Cielo, twenty-four copies, five etchings of his own, on artisanal Fabriano Perusia paper. Twenty-four copies will not pay a printing bill, and the money for this one is his own. Alberti is in Buenos Aires in these years, a Spanish republican in exile, and the poem is early Alberti, out of the surrealist decade. The house history claims four decades of work under this name, and the twenty-four copies are where it starts.
suggested_refs: Rafael Alberti, Tres Recuerdos del Cielo, Ediciones Urania, Buenos Aires 1943, 24 copies

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the hands that were not his
stops.date_confidence: same event as the stop above, split out for the correction it carries. The date is placement, not record.
stops.campa: The house history is exact about the division of labor, and the exactness corrects him downward: Alejandro Zampieri composes the text in movable lead type, Emilio Colombo prints it, and the whole is produced at the printing house of Don Francisco Colombo under the care of the poet Basilio Uribe. Veroni finances, commissions, and etches. He does not set the type and he does not pull the sheets. The Colombo press and Basilio Uribe both recur in his work for the next twenty years; the first book already contains the whole network.
stops.quote: compuesto por Alejandro Zampieri con tipos móviles de plomo, impreso por Emilio Colombo e ilustrado con 5 aguafuertes de Veroni
suggested_refs: The imprenta of Francisco A. Colombo, Buenos Aires, the press behind most Argentine bibliophile editions of the period

stops.name: Buenos Aires, one etching in Salomé
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by OpenLibrary edition OL58008884M and a bookseller's listing; no month recorded.
stops.campa: Francisco A. Colombo issues Oscar Wilde's Salomé in two volumes: three hundred numbered copies on Polar paper in two fascicles, plus twenty-eight special copies on Croxley with Fabriano and Guarro covers, numbered I to XXVIII. The scholarly version is by Aníbal Bargas Nigoul; the woodcuts are by Constante Orlando Paladino. Veroni's contribution is a single etching. He is one name among four on a book he did not design, which is what the working life of a plate-cutter looks like between the editions he owns.
stops.quote: scholarly version by Aníbal Bargas Nigoul, woodcuts by Constante Orlando Paladino, and an etching by Raúl Veroni
stops.quote_source: OpenLibrary edition record OL58008884M, Salomé, Francisco A. Colombo, 1944
suggested_refs: OpenLibrary OL58008884M, which corrects the bookseller attribution of the woodcuts
sources: AbeBooks listing, Francisco A. Colombo, Buenos Aires 1944

stops.name: Buenos Aires, an etching for Marechal
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by a bookseller's listing; the etching itself has not been examined.
stops.campa: Emecé publishes Leopoldo Marechal's El viaje de la primavera with an etching by Veroni. Marechal is three years from Adán Buenosayres, the novel that will make him the great disputed figure of Argentine letters. Emecé takes Veroni's work for the next twenty-four years, from this etching to a cover in 1969. The whole record of those twenty-four years is title pages and jackets; no contract, no letter, and no meeting between the house and the engraver survives in anything reachable.
suggested_refs: Leopoldo Marechal, El viaje de la primavera, Emecé, Buenos Aires 1945

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Miguel Mañara
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A single bookseller listing is the only witness; neither the 1947 date nor Veroni's hand is independently confirmed. The listing also carries the author's initials wrong, as O. W. rather than O. V.
stops.campa: A bookseller records an Emecé edition of Miguel Mañara by the Lithuanian-French poet Oscar Vladislas de Lubicz Milosz, illustrated by Veroni. The listing gives the initials as O. W., and no second source confirms either the year or Veroni's hand in it. The stop is entered here because the pattern fits and kept out of the attested spine because one dealer's catalogue line is not a book in front of anyone. The mystical dramatic poem of a Spanish penitent is exactly the sort of text this press liked.
suggested_refs: O. V. de Lubicz Milosz, Miguel Mañara (1935), Spanish edition attributed to Emecé 1947
sources: OpenLibrary authority record, 'Oscar Vladislas de Lubicz Milosz'

segments.name: The Colombo Years and the Small Numbers

stops.name: Buenos Aires, four plates for the Flor de la Rosa
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by a bookseller's listing.
stops.campa: Daniel Devoto compiles the Cancionero llamado Flor de la Rosa and Francisco A. Colombo prints it for Gulab y Aldabahor; Veroni engraves four plates. Devoto is a medievalist and a musicologist, and the cancionero is the kind of scholarly recovery that in Buenos Aires in 1950 comes dressed as a bibliophile object rather than an edition for students. Seven years after the first Urania book the same press is still pulling his plates, and he is still, on the title page, the engraver rather than the publisher.
suggested_refs: Cancionero llamado Flor de la Rosa, comp. Daniel Devoto, Gulab y Aldabahor / Francisco A. Colombo, 1950
sources: AbeBooks listing, Gulab y Aldabahor / Francisco A. Colombo

stops.name: Buenos Aires, L'Antico Amor in eighty-two copies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the collation, the two paper states and the copy count come from a detailed bookseller description.
stops.campa: Colombo, Urania and Raúl Veroni share the imprint on Giacomo Leopardi's L'Antico Amor: fifty-five pages, eighty-two numbered copies in two paper states, twenty-seven on Fabriano Magnani and fifty-five on Ingres. Six etchings, one of them a vignette, the frontispiece signed by him in pencil, glassine wrappers, a cartonné box. Basilio Uribe, who oversaw the Alberti eight years earlier, supplies the Spanish translation. No other edition of his survives in a description this full, and this one survives because a dealer had the object in his hands.
suggested_refs: Giacomo Leopardi, L'Antico Amor, Colombo / Urania / Raul Veroni, Buenos Aires 1951, 82 numbered copies
sources: AbeBooks listing, 'Buenos Aires Colombo Urania Raul Veroni - 1951'

stops.name: Milan, the other Urania
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Mondadori imprint's founding year. Carried as a reception hazard rather than an event in Veroni's life; he is in Buenos Aires throughout.
stops.campa: In Milan, nine years after a Buenos Aires engraver took the name of the muse of the heavens for a press of twenty-four copies, Mondadori launches a science-fiction line and calls it Urania. Giorgio Monicelli founds it in 1952; it becomes the most famous Urania in publishing and swallows the search results for the other one. The Argentine house is the earlier by nine years and is not derived from it. The collision is recorded here as a hazard for anyone hunting Veroni's imprint by name, and nothing more: the two cities share the word and, in him, a birth certificate.
suggested_refs: Urania (Mondadori), Milan, founded 1952 by Giorgio Monicelli
sources: researcher background knowledge, flagged as unverified in this session

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Shelley in sixty-three copies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by the house blog, which describes a surviving numbered copy; no month recorded.
stops.campa: For the poetry collection La Cabellera he edits and illustrates Shelley bilingually: A una alondra facing To a Skylark, translated by Juan Rodolfo Wilcock, with an engraving of his own, sixty-three numbered copies on Ingres Écoles paper. Wilcock at this point is a Buenos Aires poet in the orbit of Silvina Ocampo and Bioy Casares, some years from abandoning Spanish for Italian and leaving Argentina for good. Veroni, Italian by birth, is printing Wilcock's Spanish; Wilcock will end his life writing in Veroni's first language.
stops.quote_source: edicionesurania.blogspot.com, description of a surviving copy of the 1955 Shelley
suggested_refs: A una alondra / To a Skylark, trans. Juan Rodolfo Wilcock, Colección de Poesía La Cabellera, 1955, 63 copies
sources: edicionesurania.blogspot.com, post on the Shelley edition

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the roll of the house
stops.date_confidence: span, not an event. The source gives no years at all; 1955 is the midpoint of the four decades the house claims, chosen for placement only.
stops.campa: The house's own account of four decades names its poets in one breath: Enrique Banchs, Alfonsina Storni, Silvina Ocampo, Tulio Carella, Shelley, T. S. Eliot, Edgar Allan Poe, Leopardi, Sappho. It is a list of texts, not of collaborators. Storni drowned herself at Mar del Plata in 1938, five years before Urania existed; Poe and Leopardi and Sappho are further out of reach still. Only Banchs, Silvina Ocampo and Carella were alive and in the city, and no reachable source records Veroni speaking to any of them.
stops.quote: con poetas de la estatura de Enrique Banchs, Alfonsina Storni, Silvina Ocampo, Tulio Carella, Shelley, T. S. Eliot, Edgar Allan Poe, Leopardi, Safo entre muchos otros
stops.quote_source: edicionesurania.blogspot.com, exhibition notice for 'El libro como arte'
suggested_refs: The full Ediciones Urania backlist, never catalogued in any reachable bibliography

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a vignette for Molinari
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by a bookseller's listing.
stops.campa: Emecé publishes Ricardo E. Molinari's Días Donde la Tarde es un Pájaro with a cover vignette and a drawing by Veroni. Molinari is the most private of the great Argentine poets of the century, a man who printed much of his own work in tiny editions and disliked being read in public. The commission is characteristic of the second half of Veroni's working life: not a bibliophile edition of his own, but the cover of another house's trade book, done well enough that a bookseller sixty years later still names him on it.
suggested_refs: Ricardo E. Molinari, Días Donde la Tarde es un Pájaro, Emecé, 1954

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La Niña de la Rosa
stops.date_confidence: year attested by OpenLibrary and a bookseller's listing; the month is placement only. The author's name reached this atlas inverted and is corrected here.
stops.campa: He illustrates La Niña de la Rosa for Emecé. The author is Fermín Estrella Gutiérrez, born in Spain in 1900 and resident in Argentina, a schoolteacher-poet whose books furnished a generation of Argentine classrooms. His name has sometimes been printed inverted, as Estrella Fermín Gutiérrez; the correct order is Fermín Estrella Gutiérrez. He dies in 1990, two years before Veroni. The two are near-exact contemporaries who shared a publisher and, so far as any reachable source says, nothing else.
suggested_refs: Fermín Estrella Gutiérrez (1900-1990), La niña de la rosa, Emecé, 1955

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a cover for Criterio
stops.date_confidence: year attested by a bookseller's listing; the month is placement, chosen to sit beside the events the campa names.
stops.campa: Ediciones Criterio publishes La Democracia Cristiana by Gustavo J. Franceschi with a cover designed by Veroni. Franceschi runs Criterio, the Catholic review that is at this moment one of the loudest voices in the collision between the Church and Perón, and the year is 1955: the year the collision ends with bombs over the Plaza de Mayo and a general in the Casa Rosada. Veroni's hand is on the jacket of a political tract in the middle of it. Nothing in any reachable source records an opinion of his.
suggested_refs: Gustavo J. Franceschi, La Democracia Cristiana, Ediciones Criterio, 1955

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Los Altares
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by a bookseller's listing.
stops.campa: Emecé publishes Pedro Miguel Obligado's Los Altares with illustrations by Veroni. Obligado is by now an old man of the Argentine academy, son of a poet, holder of the national poetry prize, a figure from a Buenos Aires literary generation older than Veroni's own. This is the first of two Obligado books in the record. The second will appear four years after Obligado is dead, with a Veroni engraving in it and Veroni's own studio on the imprint, and no one alive on the poet's side of the page.
suggested_refs: Pedro Miguel Obligado (1892-1967), Los Altares, Emecé, 1959

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Los Días
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A single bookseller listing is the only witness to the vignette; the month is placement only.
stops.campa: A bookseller records Emecé's Los Días by Basilio Uribe with a cover vignette by Veroni. Uribe is the poet who oversaw the Alberti of 1943 and translated the Leopardi of 1951. If the listing is right, the two men are still working together sixteen years on with the roles reversed: the overseer is now the author and the financier is now the jacket artist. No second source confirms it, so the stop is carried as reconstruction. What hangs on it is sixteen unbroken years between the same two men.
suggested_refs: Basilio Uribe, Los Días, Emecé, 1959

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Imposturas
stops.date_confidence: year attested by a bookseller's listing. The Borges connection in the campa is researcher background, not from the verified pool.
stops.campa: Emecé publishes Betina Edelberg's Imposturas with a cover illustration by Veroni. Edelberg is remembered outside her own books as a collaborator of Jorge Luis Borges, with whom she wrote a study of Leopoldo Lugones in 1955; the borges journey holds the same Buenos Aires pin as this stop. She is one of several people here whose names sit one step from the center of Argentine letters. Veroni is on their covers for twenty-five years without a single reachable source placing him inside a room with any of them.
suggested_refs: Betina Edelberg, Imposturas, Emecé, 1960; and Borges and Edelberg, Leopoldo Lugones, 1955
sources: researcher background knowledge for the Borges collaboration, unverified this session

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El Río de los Años
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by a bookseller's listing.
stops.campa: León Benarós publishes El Río de los Años with Emecé and a cover vignette by Veroni. Benarós is a poet, a folklorist and a historian of the Argentine interior, one of the writers who spent a life collecting what the capital forgets. The vignette is small work. The point of listing it is the pattern: between 1954 and 1969 the same engraver marks at least nine Emecé books, which makes him, with no title anywhere saying so, part of the visual signature of an Argentine publishing house.
suggested_refs: León Benarós, El Río de los Años, Emecé, 1964

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Poemas entre dos Eras
stops.date_confidence: year attested by a bookseller's listing; the month is placement only, set after the Benarós cover for ordering.
stops.campa: The second Emecé cover of the year goes on Horacio Moine Macías's Poemas entre dos Eras. Nothing about the poet is recoverable from any source reachable for this journey beyond his name on the title page and Veroni's vignette beneath it. The stop stands anyway. The book was printed in Buenos Aires, sold, and then catalogued once by a dealer sixty years later. Most of the working life recorded in this journey survives on exactly that thread, one dealer at a time.
suggested_refs: Horacio Moine Macías, Poemas entre dos Eras, Emecé, 1964

segments.name: Raúl Veroni Editor, and the Estudio Gráfico

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Carducci under his own name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by a bookseller's listing, which gives the two paper states and the copy count.
stops.campa: Under the imprint Raúl Veroni Editor, his own name standing alone where Urania used to stand, he publishes Poemas by Giosuè Carducci with an original lithograph signed by him: one hundred and twenty-five copies, two on Rives and one hundred and twenty-three on Ingres. Carducci is the first Italian to take the Nobel, dead since 1907, a poet of the Risorgimento's classical wing. At fifty-two, in Buenos Aires, the Milanese engraver is still publishing Italians into Spanish and still counting his copies in the dozens.
suggested_refs: Giosuè Carducci, Poemas, Raúl Veroni Editor, Buenos Aires 1965, 125 copies

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Cuadernos de Arte, Mendoza I
stops.date_confidence: 1967 per the bookseller's record. The research pool that reached this atlas gave 1966 and called Veroni the publisher; both are corrected, and the correction is logged in the report.
stops.campa: The Centro de Medios Audiovisuales de la República Argentina presents the first Mendoza notebook of the Cuadernos de Arte, printed at the Estudio Gráfico de Raúl Veroni in an edition of two hundred: Roberto Azzoni, Federico Céspedes, Zdravko Ducmelic, Dardo Retamoza, Juan Scalco. Ducmelic is a Croatian who reached Argentina after the war and made Mendoza his country, which is the same shape of life as the printer's. An earlier pass dated the notebook 1966; the record says 1967.
suggested_refs: Cuadernos de Arte, Mendoza I, Estudio Gráfico de Raúl Veroni, 1967, 200 copies
sources: AbeBooks listing, Estudio Gráfico de Raúl Veroni

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Cuadernos de Arte, Córdoba I
stops.date_confidence: year attested by a bookseller's listing; the month is placement only.
stops.campa: A second notebook in the same series, this one for Córdoba, comes off the same studio press in the same edition of two hundred. The Cuadernos are a provincial art survey printed in the capital: living painters from Mendoza and Córdoba reproduced properly, in a run small enough to be handled and large enough to be sent out. Veroni is fifty-four, and the studio that pulls these sheets carries his own name on the door. The bibliophile publisher of twenty-four copies is now a jobbing printer of two hundred, and both trades are his.
suggested_refs: Cuadernos de Arte, Córdoba I, Estudio Gráfico de Raúl Veroni, 1967, 200 copies
sources: AbeBooks listing, Estudio Gráfico de Raúl Veroni

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Premio Emecé cover
stops.date_confidence: year attested by a bookseller's listing, which also names the prize; the month is placement only.
stops.campa: Clara Bottini's Caza Mayor wins the Premio Emecé for 1967 and goes out with a cover illustration by Veroni. It is the only prize anywhere in this record and it is not his: the award belongs to the novel and the engraver is on the jacket. Twenty-four years after twenty-four copies of Alberti, his hand is on a book that a national publishing prize has just put into every bookshop window in Buenos Aires. No source records what he was paid for the drawing, or whether he read the novel.
suggested_refs: Clara Bottini, Caza Mayor, Emecé, 1967, Premio Emecé 1967

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Levántate y Canta
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A single dealer listing is the only witness to the vignette and nothing confirms it.
stops.campa: A dealer records Emecé's Levántate y Canta by Rodolfo E. Modern with a cover vignette by Veroni. Modern is a Germanist and a poet who will go on to the Academia Argentina de Letras. The listing is the only witness, so the stop is carried as reconstruction. Emecé is by this point his oldest client, twenty-three years on from the Marechal etching, which is why the attribution is plausible and not why it is proved. Dropping the weak entries would make the record look firmer than it is.
suggested_refs: Rodolfo E. Modern, Levántate y Canta, Emecé, 1968

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the last Emecé vignette
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by a bookseller's listing.
stops.campa: Federico Peltzer's La mi Muerte appears from Emecé with a cover vignette by Veroni, the last of the Emecé jobs in the reachable record. Peltzer is a lawyer and novelist of the Catholic literary circles the Criterio cover of 1955 already touched. The house that took his etching when he was thirty-two takes his last vignette at fifty-six. Fifteen years of covers end here with no farewell and no sign in the record that either party thought a chapter was closing.
suggested_refs: Federico Peltzer, La mi Muerte, Emecé, 1969

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Mendoza II in fifty copies
stops.date_confidence: year attested by a bookseller's listing; the month is placement only.
stops.campa: The second Mendoza notebook comes off his studio press in fifty copies, a quarter of the run of the first. Nothing in the record explains the reduction: whether the series was failing, whether the paper was short, whether fifty was simply what the sponsor paid for. The number is worth keeping because Veroni's whole working life is legible in his print runs. Twenty-four, sixty-three, eighty-two, one hundred and twenty-five, two hundred, fifty: it is the only continuous series of quantities he left behind.
suggested_refs: Cuadernos de Arte, Mendoza II, Estudio Gráfico de Raúl Veroni, 1969, 50 copies
sources: AbeBooks listing, Estudio Gráfico de Raúl Veroni

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El Andén without its poet
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by a bookseller's listing. Obligado's death in 1967 is attested separately, which makes the volume posthumous.
stops.campa: El Andén appears under a joint imprint, Obligado together with the Estudio Gráfico Raúl Veroni, reproducing one of Veroni's engravings. Pedro Miguel Obligado has been dead since 1967. The book is a posthumous issue and cannot be narrated as a collaboration between living men: twelve years after Los Altares the engraver puts a plate into the poet's last book, and the poet is not there to see which plate it is. An earlier pass did not note the death; the correction stands.
stops.quote: Con una reproducción de un grabado de Raúl Veroni
stops.quote_source: AbeBooks listing for El Andén, Obligado / Estudio Gráfico Raúl Veroni, 1971
suggested_refs: Pedro Miguel Obligado, El Andén, 1971, issued four years after the author's death
sources: AbeBooks listing, Obligado / Estudio Gráfico Raúl Veroni

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La Luz que Más Me Vale
stops.date_confidence: year attested by a bookseller's listing; the month is placement only.
stops.campa: Nexo publishes Horacio Esteban Ratti's La Luz que Más Me Vale with illustrations by Veroni. Ratti is a poet of the countryside and a past president of the Argentine writers' society, another establishment figure whose book passes through Veroni's hands without leaving a trace of the man in any memoir. He is fifty-eight. The imprint is new, the poet is familiar in kind, and the work is the work it has been since 1940: someone needs a plate, and he cuts it.
suggested_refs: Horacio Esteban Ratti, La Luz que Más Me Vale, Nexo, Buenos Aires 1971

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Hospital de Niños in two hundred copies
stops.date_confidence: 1976 per the bookseller's record, which gives the collation and the run. The research pool dated this 1969; seven years is too large an error to carry silently, so the later date stands and the discrepancy is logged.
stops.campa: A second edition of Oscar R. C. Vogliano's Hospital de Niños is printed in Buenos Aires with engravings by Veroni: one hundred and thirty-six pages, sixteen by twenty-three and a half centimetres, two hundred copies. A book about a children's hospital, issued in two hundred copies with original engravings, is not a commercial object. It is a monument somebody paid for. The engraver is sixty-two and the commission is the same commission it always was, aimed this time at a building full of sick children.
stops.quote_source: AbeBooks listing for Oscar R. C. Vogliano, Hospital de Niños, second edition, Buenos Aires 1976
suggested_refs: Oscar R. C. Vogliano, Hospital de Niños, second edition, Buenos Aires 1976, 200 copies

stops.name: San Juan, drawings for El Regalo
stops.date_confidence: year attested by a bookseller's listing; the month is placement only. The inscription described is on one copy, not in the edition.
stops.campa: Cooedit of San Juan, in the Andean west, publishes Antonio de la Torre's El Regalo, Cuentos y Narraciones, one hundred and twenty-eight pages with drawings by Veroni. One surviving copy carries an inscription in the author's own hand to el artista Raúl Veroni. The dedication is a manuscript on that copy and not a printed dedication of the edition, and the distinction is kept here. It is the only stop in this journey that leaves Buenos Aires after 1940, and it leaves only as far as a provincial press with his drawings in it.
stops.quote: inscribed and signed by the author... al artista Raúl Veroni
stops.quote_source: AbeBooks listing for Antonio de la Torre, El Regalo, Cooedit, San Juan 1976
suggested_refs: Antonio de la Torre, El Regalo, Cuentos y Narraciones, Cooedit, San Juan 1976
sources: AbeBooks listing, Cooedit, San Juan, Argentina

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the last dated work
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by a bookseller's listing. It is the last dated item in the reachable file; the fourteen years after it are blank.
stops.campa: Antonio Requeni publishes the thirtieth number of Hojas de Poesía at his own expense, illustrated by Veroni. Requeni is a poet and a journalist of La Prensa who will outlast almost everyone else in this record. It is the last dated work in the reachable file. Veroni is sixty-five with fourteen years still to live, and the sources go quiet at this point: no exhibitions, no late editions, no interviews, no obituary, nothing at all between this pamphlet and a line of catalogue data giving the year he died.
suggested_refs: Antonio Requeni, Hojas de Poesía No. 30, edición del autor, Buenos Aires 1978

stops.name: Buenos Aires, death without a grave in the record
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year and the city only. LoC no2023125659 records deathDate 1992 and mads:deathPlace Buenos Aires; no month, no day. The cemetery, grave and any monument are a flat gap: no funerary record of any kind surfaced.
stops.campa: He dies in Buenos Aires. No month is recorded, no day, no cemetery, no plot, no monument. The Library of Congress holds the place and the year and nothing further, sourced to an Argentine art reference a cataloguer consulted in November 2023, thirty-one years after the fact. A man who spent fifty years making objects whose whole purpose was to be permanent and countable left behind a death that cannot be dated closer than a year. The workshop, the Casa-Taller, stays in the family.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a 1955 Shelley rebound by other hands
stops.date_confidence: no year is attested; the source gives none. 2010 is a placeholder standing for 'contemporary, after Veroni's death', not a claim about when the binding was made. The research pool folded this into the 1955 edition and produced an anachronism; it is split out here.
stops.campa: One copy of the 1955 Shelley, number sixteen of sixty-three, is rebound by the Argentine binder Sol Rebora in her Estructura Francesa: goat leather, with reversible Japanese-paper escartivanas. Rebora is a contemporary craftswoman and this is a later artisanal rebinding, no part of Veroni's own production. Sixty-three copies is a small enough run that a single one can still be tracked by its number seventy years later. This one is number sixteen, and the newest work on it is not his.
suggested_refs: Sol Rebora's Estructura Francesa binding of a copy of the 1955 Veroni Shelley

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Avenida Las Heras 2555: El libro como arte
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The exhibition blog gives the opening as Thursday 9 August 2012 at 7 pm, the close as 15 December, and the hours as Tuesday to Sunday, 2 to 7. Coordinates are derived from the street address, not from a gazetteer entry for the museum.
stops.campa: Twenty years after his death the Museo del Libro y de la Lengua opens its Veroni show at Avenida Las Heras 2555. The doors open on a Thursday evening at seven and the exhibition runs to the fifteenth of December, Tuesday to Sunday, two until seven. On the walls: typographic compositions, xylographic blocks, colophons, all carried out of the Casa-Taller where he worked. It is the only public reckoning with him in the reachable record, and the address is the only place in this journey that can be found to the street number.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the documentary and the second Raúl Veroni
stops.date_confidence: the documentary accompanies the 2012 exhibition; no separate release date is recorded, and the day here is placement immediately after the opening.
stops.campa: The museum makes a documentary for the show and fills it with the trade rather than with critics: Alejandro Geiler, who makes paper; Patricio Gatti, who prints; Lorena Pradal, who engraves; Leandro Jacob and Martín Artagaveytia, who edit and print. And Raúl Veroni, who carries the same name and keeps the same workshop. Two men, one name, one Casa-Taller. The younger Raúl Veroni carries the family name and the workshop forward; the exact relation between the two is documented only by the shared name and the continuity of the studio.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the pin his son will share
stops.date_confidence: atlas-internal. This is the date of the corpus census that placed the Veroni family in the atlas, not an event in Veroni's life.
stops.campa: Buenos Aires holds his fifty-two working years at one address, from the crossing out of Milan to the death recorded without a grave. Ediciones Urania, the house he founded on twenty-four copies of Alberti, later published Silvina Ocampo among its poets, though no reachable source places the two of them in a room together. His son and namesake carries the family name and the Casa-Taller forward after him. Arthur Ben's own essay, written from outside the family, imagines a second life spent in this city as this quiet engraver's friend.
stops.quote: inherited byte for byte, already shared by eight other journeys
